opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they go deeper than people usually expect.

The first is that a lot of the questions we're now asking in AI are really old questions wearing new clothes. What does it mean to understand something? Is there a difference between predicting the next word and actually knowing what you're talking about? What counts as reasoning? Philosophers have been arguing about these things for centuries, and many of the positions people stake out on Twitter about whether large models "really" think were already articulated, and often refuted or refined, decades ago. Searle's Chinese Room, Wittgenstein on meaning as use, the debates between rationalists and empiricists. These map surprisingly well onto the debate between people who believe scale alone gets you intelligence and people who think you need built-in structure. If you don't know that history, you end up reinventing arguments, and usually weaker versions of them.

The second reason is about concepts. Research progress often depends less on clever engineering than on asking the right question, and philosophy is basically training in sharpening concepts. When we talk about "alignment," aligned to what? Whose values? Values as stated preferences, or as what people would want on reflection? Those distinctions sound academic until you try to write a reward function, and then suddenly they're the whole problem. Moral philosophy gives you a vocabulary for that: consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, the problems of aggregating preferences. You don't have to pick a side, but you should know where the landmines are.

Third, philosophy of mind and epistemology make you more careful about evaluation. We build benchmarks and then declare a model has some capability because it passed a test. But passing a test and having the capability aren't the same thing, and philosophy trains you to notice that gap, to ask what a behavior actually licenses you to infer.

And finally, I'd say it's about humility. Engineers, myself included, can fall into thinking every problem is technical. Reading philosophy reminds you that some questions, like what we want these systems to be and what kind of future we're building, aren't going to be settled by more compute. They need judgment. And if the people building the technology don't engage with those questions, someone else will answer them for us, or worse, nobody will, and the defaults will just happen.

So it's not that philosophy gives you answers. It gives you better questions, and in a field moving this fast, better questions are probably the scarcest resource.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because the questions AI keeps running into are not new questions. They're old questions wearing new clothes.

Take something as basic as "does this model understand language?" Engineers argue about it over lunch as if it's a benchmark problem, but it's really the question Wittgenstein and Searle and Quine spent their whole careers on. What does it mean to follow a rule? Can meaning come from symbol manipulation alone? If you've read that literature, you walk into the debate with a map. If you haven't, you spend a lot of time rediscovering positions that were already carefully articulated fifty or a hundred years ago, and often rediscovering them badly.

The second reason is more practical. In AI, we're constantly operationalizing concepts. We say we're measuring "reasoning," or "alignment," or "agency," and then we build a dataset and a metric. But every one of those words is doing an enormous amount of hidden work. Philosophy is basically the discipline of noticing when a word is doing hidden work and refusing to let it get away with that. Reading philosophy trains a kind of suspicion toward your own definitions, and I think that suspicion is exactly what a field moving this fast is missing.

And then there's the ethical dimension, which people usually mention first, but I'd actually put third. Yes, if you're building systems that make decisions about people, you should have thought about what a decision is, what fairness is, what it means to be responsible for an outcome. But I'd say that even setting ethics aside, philosophy makes you a better scientist here, because it makes you clearer about what claim you're actually making when you publish a result.

So my short answer is: the technical problems are hard, but the conceptual problems are harder, and we've inherited a few thousand years of people working on the conceptual ones. It would be strange not to use that.

astra-6.text:
I think AI researchers should read philosophy because many of the questions we’re working on are also philosophical questions. What is intelligence? What does it mean to understand something? What counts as knowledge? Once you try to build an intelligent system, those questions become very concrete.

Take understanding, for example. If a model gives you the right answer, does that mean it understands? How would you distinguish understanding from a very convincing imitation? Before you design an experiment, you already need some idea of what you mean by those terms. Philosophy helps you examine those assumptions.

It also teaches you to take an argument apart: What are the premises? Does the conclusion actually follow? Are we disagreeing about the evidence, or just using the same word in different ways? That’s useful in a field where people can look at the same model and reach completely different conclusions.

I wouldn’t say philosophy gives us a blueprint for building AI. Its value is that it helps us ask clearer questions—and recognize when a technical result doesn’t quite answer the question we thought we were asking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI research brings us back to questions philosophy has been asking for a long time: What is knowledge? What does it mean to understand something? What counts as intelligence? When we build a system, we inevitably make assumptions about those questions, even if we never state them explicitly.

For example, if a model gives the correct answer, does that mean it understands? Before we can design an experiment to test that, we need to clarify what we mean by “understanding.” Philosophy helps us examine the question itself, instead of immediately looking for a technical solution.

It also helps us think about objectives. We spend a lot of effort asking how to make a system better at achieving a goal. But why is that the right goal? Whose values does it reflect? Those questions become more important as these systems become more capable.

So I wouldn’t say researchers should read philosophy because it gives them ready-made answers. Its value is that it teaches you to recognize your assumptions, make clearer distinctions, and ask better questions.
